commit_reviews.summary: Faithfully executes the mandated Session 4 Repository refactor — all SQLite access moves into TaskRepository/UserRepository behind a BaseRepository ABC and routes now delegate cleanly to repository methods.

compounding_issues: Session 1 moved init_db() to import time; the resulting import-time side effect (schema creation + legacy-user seeding) persisted into every later session and becomes an implicit startup contract that breaks if app.py is ever imported without a writable DATABASE

Session 2 introduced a freeform 'status' string with no enum constraint; Session 3 and 5 rely on string equality against 'completed', so a status like 'Completed' would silently skip the notification hook

Session 5's cursor pagination changed GET /tasks from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking API shape change that would break any existing client, even though tests were updated consistently
Session 3 committed __pycache__/*.pyc artifacts, which kept getting re-committed and churned the diff across sessions instead of being gitignored
key_decisions: Session 2: adding JWT auth with per-owner task ownership (owner_id) and a 'legacy' migration user — this single decision re-shaped every later session's queries, endpoints, and tests
Session 4: extracting a BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository data-access layer, slimming app.py by ~126 lines and decoupling SQL from the HTTP layer
Session 3: integrating Celery with a decoupled tasks module for async completion notifications, keeping the mock outside the request path
Session 5: introducing cursor-based pagination (limit/cursor/total) and Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed by authenticated subject
Keeping SQLite with idempotent ALTER TABLE migrations inside init_db() — a simple, test-friendly schema evolution strategy that survived all five sessions
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 was modest hardening (strict validation, timezone-corrected timestamps, import-time init). Session 2 delivered the biggest step — JWT auth, users, and per-owner task isolation — which became the backbone for everything after. Session 3 layered in async Celery notifications, Session 4 was a clean structural refactor that moved data access into repositories and actually reduced app.py size while preserving behavior, and Session 5 added production-grade cross-cutting concerns (pagination, rate limiting, 429 handling). Each session shipped with tests and the final suite (9 tests, growing from the initial 5) passes cleanly. The only quality dips are the Session 5 breaking response-shape change and a smattering of committed .pyc artifacts, but overall the code grew more structured, more feature-complete, and better tested over time.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-orchestrated story where a deliberate ownership+auth foundation (S2) was cleanly refactored (S4) and topped with production hardening (S5), with consistent test coverage throughout and no early decision that critically compromised later sessions.
